blocks.text: Alkhabeer Diversified Income Traded Fund (“the Fund”) is a closed-ended Shari’a-compliant investment traded fund established in accordance with the applicable laws and regulations of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and regulated by the Capital Market Authority (CMA). The Fund’s investment objective is to generate periodic income to investors by investing in Shari’a-compliant income generating assets. The Fund Manager “Alkhabeer Capital” plans to invest in Sukuk, trade finance transactions, leasing transactions, income funds and Murabaha transactions, either directly or through investment funds.

4. Standard Deviation is a measure of risk. It is calculated as any volatility in returns over a period of time. The lower the volatility, the more homogeneous the set of returns.
5. Sharpe Ratio is a risk-adjusted performance measure. It is calculated as the difference as the Fund Manager excess return over the risk-free rate, divided by the Standard Deviation. The greater a portfolio's Sharpe Ratio, the better its risk-adjusted performance.
6. Tracking Error is a measure of risks. It is calculated as the Standard Deviation between the Fund Manager's return and the Benchmark's return. The lower the Tracking Error, the lower the Fund Manager deviates from the Benchmark.
7. Beta is a measure of the average historical sensitivity of the Fund's returns compared to market returns. It is calculated by using the covariance of the Fund and the market on the variance of the market.
8. Alpha measures any excess return achieved by the Fund compared to the performance of the index.
9. Information Ratio is a risk-adjusted performance measure. It is calculated as the active return of the Fund Manager, divided by its tracking error. The higher the Information ratio, the higher the Fund Manager ability to generate excess returns per Unit of excess risk. Knowing that the performance and risk parameters were calculated based on the Unit's trading prices in the market.

OVERVIEW OF THE LEASING, TRADE FINANCE AND SUKUK INDUSTRIES

items: During Q3 of 2022, higher inflation in global economies has led to the slowdown of growth. However, strong labor market information has somewhat offset the effect on the leasing sector. As a result, the Monthly Leasing and Finance Index (MLFI-25) which reports the economic activity from 25 companies representing a cross section of the US$ 900 billion US leasing sector, has shown that their overall new business volume for July 2021 was US$ 10.1 billion, up 2% annually compared to the overall new business volume for July 2021. The cumulative new business volume was up 5% year-to-date, compared to 2021.

Meanwhile, the Monthly Confidence Index for the Equipment Finance Industry released by the Equipment Leasing and Finance Foundation (MCI-EFI) has improved to 50 in August 2022 from 46.1 in July 2022 in spite of higher interest rates, continued supply chain disruptions and higher inflation, the leasing sector continues to provide value to companies who rely on it in the procurement of capital equipment necessary for their operations.

ELFA continues to note strong interest from business and agricultural companies and producers, while they look to expand their operations and secure low rates in the long term. Demand exceeds supply as the industry continues to face delays in equipment delivery due to persisting supply chain challenges.

According to the latest estimate released by the UNCTAD, the value of world trade increased by approximately 15% to US$ 7.7 trillion in the first quarter of 2022. The most recent data for the second quarter of 2022 released by S&P Global Market Intelligence points to the positive growth of exports and imports on an annualized basis in all of the top ten countries tracked by UNCTAD.

Globally, banks are ratcheting up funds for the global commodities, according to an article recently published by Bloomberg, considering that trade finance is the lifeblood of the commodities industry, and with prices surging amid the war in Ukraine, and with the supply routes disrupted by the conflict, traders are clamoring for additional funds to pay for shipments of grains, metals and fuels.

The latest report by Trade Finance Global (TFG) focused on the viability of SME trade finance from a European outlook, pointing out that despite high inflation, record high energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty, demand for trade finance by SME’s is on the rise.

Global Sukuk issuance slowed down in the first half of 2022 in spite of the strong activity of the issuers during the first quarter, amid high demand from foreign investors. Global Sukuk raised US$ 22 billion in the first half of 2022, down by 10% from US$ 33.2 billion in the first half of 2021.

According to Moody’s Credit Ratings, global Sukuk issuance is expected to decrease from US$ 181 billion in 2021 to between US$ 160 billion and US$ 170 billion in 2022. According to Refinitiv, global Sukuk issuance is expected to slightly decrease to US$ 185 billion in 2022. Subsequently, issuance is expected to grow by 6.4% per annum over the next five years, to reach US$ 257 billion in 2027.

In terms of performance, the huge losses in the global bonds market in 2022 will mark the worst year on record since decades. The Sukuk market has declined significantly year-to-date, with the Dow Jones Sukuk Index losing 9.63% year-to-date.
